entries.title: ComEd customers pay billions to keep the lights on during storms. Will it be enough?
entries.summary: <p>ComEd customers have footed the bill for billions of dollars spent by the utility in recent years to help ensure that power stays on in Northern Illinois even during the worst weather.</p><p>Yet the lights still went out in 2.4 million homes during storms this year. Sometimes, it was for an hour or less. But people in the south suburbs have been left without electricity for as long as five days.</p><p>Keeping the power on during increasingly extreme weather costs a lot. As a result, ComEd says it needs to raise more than $15 billion through rate increases so it can handle rising demand and deal with intense storms that experts say are getting worse because of climate change.</p><p>That’s on top of $4.4 billion being spent on a previously approved initiative to strengthen the electric grid — the system of lines, towers, poles and other equipment connecting power plants to homes and businesses. As a regulated utility, ComEd has to apply to the state of Illinois for any rate increases. And it has done so regularly over the past couple of decades.</p><p>It's a cost that hopefully pays off.</p><p>To see what's at stake, consider what happened recently in Gary, where <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/morning-edition/2026/08/24/gary-northwest-indiana-chicago-public-schools-cook-county-property-taxes" >people were left helpless</a> as a storm with the velocity of a Category 2 hurricane tore through the city, knocking out power for two weeks. Many blamed the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/23/lawsuit-nipsco-neglected-power-lines-hazard-trees-storms-northwest-indiana-weather-electricity" >In a lawsuit,</a> Northwest Indiana residents say the electric utility, known as NIPSCO, didn't protect its power lines and utility poles from tree damage ahead of the storms. NIPSCO disputes that.</p><p>"Gary should be a warning to all utilities — in Illinois and across the nation," said Sarah Moskowitz, executive director of the Illinois watchdog group the Citizens Utility Board. "It's their duty to cost-effectively maintain the system and preserve affordability. If that duty takes a backseat to their profit margin, they risk disaster."</p><p>In <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/englewood" >Englewood</a> in June, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/12/chicago-severe-weather-tornadoes-power-outage-comed-customers-englewood" >more than 900 ComEd customers lost power</a> for three or four days after a storm downed thousands of trees, complicating repairs. ComEd said its goal is to restore power in 12 to 24 hours after the most severe storms, but damage from such extreme weather can make that difficult.</p><p>In Chicago this year, ComEd said it has had 336,000 outages, most on the South Side and the Southwest Side.</p><p>For Renee Rudder, who has lived in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/south-deering" >South Deering</a> for 36 years, power outages from storms have become a routine problem. Rudder said she lost electricity for a day and a half in July after one storm but faced a longer outage after a storm last summer that forced her to throw out $400 worth of groceries.</p><p>“We have a supply of flashlights and batteries and candles,” she said.</p><p>Still, she realizes people in Gary have had things much worse.</p><p>“I’m complaining about the three or four days, while they have been out two weeks," Rudder said. "I try to count my blessings."</p><h3><b>Record year for storms</b></h3><p>ComEd has 1.4 million customers in Chicago among the 4 million across its service area. It has had a busy year due to thunderstorms, tornadoes and furious winds. It’s already been the worst year for big storms, but not for total power outages, according to the company, which said it had nearly 3 million outages in 2011.</p><p>ComEd said the number of outages this year would be more than double what it's been had it not made technology improvements in recent years to better deal with weather-related damage. Those steps helped avoid about 2.7 million additional outages this year, according to Dale Player, the utility’s vice president of engineering and "smart grid." He said its upgrades include adding more than 10,000 devices that can automatically sense a power disturbance, isolate the problem and restore electricity.</p><p>Weather planning and response is now a big part of what ComEd does. The utility has its own staff meteorologist to anticipate severe weather.</p><p>It also is working with Argonne National Laboratory to better understand the impact of climate change on the electric grid.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7a0000" name="image-7a0000"></a> <picture officials say more must be done to strengthen parts of the grid that are many decades old.</p><p>Electric grid reliability is among the top priorities for the state utility regulator, known as the Illinois Commerce Commission, according to a spokesperson.</p><p>ComEd is required by law to point out to the state its weakest spots across Chicago and the rest of its service area, which covers } </style> </div> </div><b>Sources:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php" target="_blank" >U.S. Energy Information Administration</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.need.org/" target="_blank" >National Energy Education Development Project</a><br><b>Graphic:</b> Justin Myers/Chicago Public Media</div> </div><p>“The neighborhoods singled out in the report have circuits that had issues across multiple years of reporting,” said Thuis, Midwest regional director for the not-for-profit Carbon League. "So [they] would be the highest priority for intervention.”</p><p>That doesn't necessarily mean those areas face the prospect of a disaster like that seen in Gary. But extreme storms and aging mechanics don’t bode well for many neighborhoods. As a result of this study, ComEd has targeted these areas ahead of powerful storms.</p><h3><b>Chicago ‘franchise agreement’</b></h3><p>Since 1999, when then-Mayor Richard M. Daley blasted the utility for widespread blackouts during a heat wave, the company has stepped up investments in its infrastructure, technology and preparedness, all funded with its electricity customers’ money.</p><p>The state, not the city, regulates ComEd. But Daley cited the utility’s poor performance in saying the utility breached a long-term franchise agreement Chicago had with ComEd to provide electricity. That deal expired at the end of 2020. Despite then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot’s vows to extract more promises from ComEd, the arrangement never was renegotiated. So the utility continues to operate in Chicago under terms of the expired agreement.</p><p>“The city continues to have productive conversations,” a City Hall spokesperson said of that situation.</p><p>Ald. Matt Martin (47th) said Mayor Brandon Johnson should make reaching a new agreement with ComEd a priority.</p><p>“There could be and should be an agreement that holds ComEd accountable,” Martin said. “We definitely want to avoid what happened in Gary.”</p>

entries.title: My nearly bulletproof love for Kanye has eroded
entries.summary: <p>The first rap song I memorized was “Gold Digger.” The chop of Jamie Foxx’s crooning banged out the speakers of my family’s Honda. From there, I probably have listened to every Kanye West verse from “The College Dropout” to “The Life of Pablo.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-portrait-right> <div class="Enhancement-item" </div> </div><p>I’m a first-generation Chicagoan, born and raised. I grew up in Chatham off 79th and Cottage Grove, and Kanye’s mother, Ms. Donda West, was a family friend. “Amazing” and “Touch the Sky” played on every pre-game car ride to middle school soccer and basketball games. When I was doing poetry slam in high school, “Champion” would get played after every bout we won. He inspired the earliest days of my writing journey. Kanye’s persona — which felt genuine even with all the bravado — and his music meant something to me.</p><p>So his fall from grace has been hard to watch. When he stood with Donald Trump, I felt betrayed and bamboozled. We’ve come a long way from Kanye saying "George Bush doesn’t care about Black people,” and now I feel like he doesn’t care about Black people — or really anyone but himself. After that, I unfollowed him on all platforms and boycotted his music for years.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Getty Images for DailyWire+</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>From saying slavery was a choice, to wearing a "White Lives Matter" shirt with Candace Owens, to big-upping Adolf Hitler, to being sued for <a class="Link" href="https://people.com/kanye-west-settles-sexual-assault-lawsuit-with-former-assistant-lauren-pisciotta-12030610" target="_blank" ><u>sexual harassment</u></a> by his former assistant. … I can’t keep up. He has doubled down so emphatically on actions and rhetoric that are complete bigotry. I still don’t want to believe he believes what he’s saying and doing. “I feel the pressure under more scrutiny. And what I do? Act more stupidly!” (“Can’t Tell Me Nothing.”)</p><p>I acknowledge that he’s dealt with grief and mental health struggles, but those are not excuses for the racist, hateful and violent comments he’s made. Holding Kanye accountable comes with hopes he would apologize for and change his behavior. Unfortunately, it’s been a decade now, and not much has changed.</p><p>I watched the “Touch The Sky” music video for the first time in a while. Kanye cosplays Evel Knievel and takes the Death Rocket to touch the sky, only for the rocket to plummet and explode. I think this foreshadowed his career. He indeed touched the sky — global superstardom, financial freedom, accolades galore, undeniable musical influence on generations to come. But once he did, he fell even further.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YkwQbuAGLj4?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Kanye West - Touch The Sky (MTV Version) ft. Lupe Fiasco"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Maybe it was childish of me to feel so connected to a stranger, but that would be dismissive of my truth. Kanye was my favorite and arguably the most impactful artist of my childhood. “Heard Em Say” is one of my favorite songs ever. I have been moved to tears by a song off every Kanye album up until “Yeezus.” I catch myself on walks or cleaning my room with the verses of “Crack Music” or “Two Words” rolling off the tongue. I watched the “Jeen-Yuhs” documentary when it dropped and was reminded of what inspired me about Kanye in the first place.</p><p>But I ain’t a kid no more.</p><p>My nearly bulletproof love for Kanye has eroded as I evolved. There are artists from my childhood/adolescence whom I am excited to hear. Kanye is no longer one of them. If this was 2016, I’d have already copped my ticket for his Soldier Field show. I won’t be at this one.</p><p><i>Nile Lansana is an interdisciplinary artist, performer and educator from Chicago’s South Side. </i></p>

entries.title: After drug arrest, calls emerge for Mark Stephens to resign as chairman of Triton College's board
entries.summary: <p>Mark Stephens, the longtime chairman of Triton College’s board of trustees, should resign his leadership position in the wake of his recent drug arrest in the suburbs, according to two colleagues on the panel.</p><p>“This is an opportunity for us to move in a different direction,” says Triton board secretary Tracy Jennings. “So I’m hopeful he would see this and decide to resign that position.”</p><p>“As a board, we can’t remove him as a trustee, he’s an elected official,” Jennings says.</p><p>But as chairman — which the seven-member board chooses, with Stephens holding that position since the early 1990s — “I’d ask for him to resign.”</p><p>Jennings, who doubles as a pastor in far southwest suburban Joliet, said calls for resignation aren't only about Stephens’ July 31 arrest during a traffic stop in far northwest suburban Harvard, where police found cannabis and a substance believed to be cocaine in his car.</p><p>“Before all of this stuff happened I had already sounded the alarm that I didn’t think we were going in the right direction,” Jennings said, pointing to a “closed-off culture” under Stephens where there’s not enough transparency and accountability. That includes board meetings that aren’t streamed live, and “condescending” treatment of students who speak during the public comment sessions of those gatherings, he said.</p><p>Also galling, Jennings said, is that Stephens is known to miss the school’s annual commencement ceremonies, with more than 2,000 students graduating this past May.</p><p>“The most important day of our students’ lives, and he doesn’t show up," Jennings said.</p><p>Stephens is the brother of Rosemont Mayor Bradley Stephens and a son of late Mayor Donald E. Stephens. He couldn’t be reached for comment.</p><p>Another Triton board member, Glover Johnson, said: “I see my responsibility is to protect public confidence in Triton and remain focused on our students, employees, taxpayers and communities. I therefore believe and respectfully hope that Mr. Stephens relinquishes the chairmanship and steps away from active board duties while this case is pending. This is not a prejudgment of guilt; it is a prudent step to prevent a personal legal matter from becoming an institutional distraction.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Datcher</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>At the very beginning of Chicago’s birth, a dinner table was built, and the meal was prepared by some of the greatest Chicago Black innovators: city founder and settler Jean Baptiste Pointe DuSable built the table; publisher and writer Ida B. Wells wove a beautiful tablecloth; Chicago Defender publisher Robert Sengstacke Abbott brought the handcrafted chairs; Illinois Black Panther Deputy Chairman Fred Hampton Sr. brought fearlessness and civil rights leader Rev. Jesse L. Jackson kept hope alive for many future diners.</p><p>This table symbolized Black pride and became a cornerstone of Chicago, where writers, artists, faith leaders, grassroots organizers and political leaders had a place.</p><p>Ye lived through an era of independence and self-discovery, with the soundtrack of Chaka Khan, Curtis Mayfield and Earth, Wind & Fire. Often the lines are blurred between the streets and the lifestyle of the working man, where gangs divided up territory, police brutality was rampant and families were striving to put food on the table. But in the same neighborhoods, Black entrepreneurship flourished, and Harold Washington became the beacon of hope as Chicago's first Black mayor. Ye was shaped by this history; this became his classroom.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5f0000" name="image-5f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/add02c2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F43%2F3c98275b4e78aff08a1f1b69a850%2F6-8-jackson-farragut-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8ca6b17/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F43%2F3c98275b4e78aff08a1f1b69a850%2F6-8-jackson-farragut-11.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/67c7b91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F43%2F3c98275b4e78aff08a1f1b69a850%2F6-8-jackson-farragut-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The 3rd Annual "Stay in School" event with Lupe Fiasco Common and Kanye West performing a mini concert at Farragut Career Academy at 2345 S. Christina." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/67c7b91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F43%2F3c98275b4e78aff08a1f1b69a850%2F6-8-jackson-farragut-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ec0e097/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F43%2F3c98275b4e78aff08a1f1b69a850%2F6-8-jackson-farragut-11.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/67c7b91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F43%2F3c98275b4e78aff08a1f1b69a850%2F6-8-jackson-farragut-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The third annual “Stay in School” event with Lupe Fiasco (from left) Kanye West and Common at Farragut Career Academy in June 2010.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Brian Jackson/Chicago Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>To understand Ye, you must understand Black Chicago and the unapologetic diaspora of our history in a noticeably segregated city.</p><p>From the beginning of his music career, Ye has framed his challenges as triumphs, from his first hit, “Through the Wire,” to his Grammy Award-winning testimony in “Jesus Walks.” His music is infectious, from his famed Sunday Service to his billion-dollar Yeezy apparel empire. The ancestors built the table of opportunity, and Ye had a place at it.</p><p>His albums mention Chicago, the beloved city that didn’t always support him earlier in his career but later became his biggest champion. Nearly 21 years later, he has sold 160 million albums worldwide. Ye’s success inspires Chicago Black youth who have traveled the same South Side streets, ridden the Red Line, and taken the Stony Island bus route.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-510000" name="image-510000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1721392/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+196/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1b%2Fbf%2F1adc6a174fdaabf2f93c327f26f5%2Fgettyimages-74116668.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fa49234/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+196/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1b%2Fbf%2F1adc6a174fdaabf2f93c327f26f5%2Fgettyimages-74116668.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/720255c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+196/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1b%2Fbf%2F1adc6a174fdaabf2f93c327f26f5%2Fgettyimages-74116668.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Dr. Donda West (R) and her son, hip-hop performer Kanye West attend a book signing for her book "Raising Kanye: Life Lessons from the Mother of a Hip-Hop Superstar" on May 9, 2007 at Borders in Los Angeles, California. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/720255c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+196/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1b%2Fbf%2F1adc6a174fdaabf2f93c327f26f5%2Fgettyimages-74116668.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e050156/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+196/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1b%2Fbf%2F1adc6a174fdaabf2f93c327f26f5%2Fgettyimages-74116668.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/720255c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+196/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1b%2Fbf%2F1adc6a174fdaabf2f93c327f26f5%2Fgettyimages-74116668.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The loss of Dr. Donda West hit home for many Chicagoans who worked with her and saw how it affected her son, Mary L. Datcher writes. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Vince Bucci/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This generation also understands the complexities of mental health better than previous ones. Sadly, we’ve witnessed Ye’s own battle with mental health over the past few years. After his mother's passing in 2007, we understood she was his rock, his muse and his truth serum. This loss hit home for many Chicagoans who worked with Dr. West and saw how it affected her son. His relationships, social media outbursts and erratic behavior have been on full public display, raising the question: “Can we separate our love of his music from his personal ideologies?”</p><p>As a Black community, we wrestle with holding our public figures accountable while reserving the right to choose who to support and forgive. We cannot erase history, but we can move forward building a stronger table.</p><p>Ye still represents Chicago — the good, bad and ugly — a humanistic reflection of himself. Black Chicago hasn’t removed his place setting at the table. But if he chooses to go off course again — we will be forced to turn off the porch light.</p><p><i>Mary L. Datcher is a seasoned journalist, communications executive and political consultant with nearly three decades in music, media and entertainment, currently serving as vice president of communications at APS & Associates.</i></p>

entries.title: Mayoral candidates decry Chicago violence ‘crisis,’ even as summer murders hit 61-year low
entries.summary: <p>Despite historically low levels of violent crime in Chicago this year, candidates trying to replace Mayor Brandon Johnson are sweeping aside the numbers in favor of anecdotes and are depicting the city as reeling in a “crisis” of gun violence and lawlessness.</p><p>Chicago had 122 murders in June, July and August, according to city and police data posted through Tuesday evening. </p><p>That’s the lowest summer total since 1965. Overall violent crime hit its lowest level last year in more than four decades. City data shows the downward trend has continued this year.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-400000" name="html-embed-module-400000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30107542"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30107542/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In their mayoral quests, nevertheless, candidates keep stoking public anxiety about violent crime.</p><p>Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza, making her second run for the office, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/in-the-loop-with-sasha-ann-simons/2026/08/04/ask-the-mayoral-candidate-susana-mendoza" target="_blank" >went on WBEZ last month</a> and said the city faced a "public safety crisis." She pointed to the Chicago Transit Authority.</p><p>“How about let’s not shoot people on the CTA,” Mendoza said. “Let’s not allow people to violate people on the CTA or set them on fire. And those are the things that are happening, unfortunately.”</p><p>FBI-classified “index” crimes at CTA locations — trains, buses, stops and all other properties — are down 29% this year through Aug. 23, according to police figures. Seven categories, ranging from thefts to shootings, are all down. Two other categories increased: There were 24 sexual assaults and four arson incidents.</p><p>Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, the best-financed mayoral candidate, pointed to shootings last weekend in an X posting: “Gun violence is more than a statistic, it’s a public health crisis that is cutting too many lives short.”</p><p>U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/in-the-loop-with-sasha-ann-simons/2026/08/19/ask-the-mayoral-candidate-mike-quigley" target="_blank" >talking up his mayoral qualifications</a> on WBEZ two weeks ago, said Chicago faced a “public safety crisis” and claimed falsely that homicides were on the rise: “They’re dipping back up, obviously.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-870000" name="html-embed-module-870000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30097743"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30097743/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>George Cardenas, a Cook County Board of Review commissioner speaking on WTTW in June, said public safety improvements would be his priority as mayor and tried to sow doubts about police department crime metrics.</p><p>“I know that people don’t feel safe, especially Downtown,” Cardenas said.</p><p>Businessman Willie Wilson’s campaign website says crimes, including smash-and-grab robberies and car thefts, “have shaken the foundation of our city.”</p><p>Chicago robberies last year were down more than 86% from their 1991 peak, according to annual Chicago police reports. More recent police data shows robberies falling sharply since a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/criminal-justice/2025/04/16/chicagos-robbery-surge-is-over" target="_blank" ><u>small surge </u>in 2022 and 2023</a> that experts tied to the pandemic.</p><p>Several lesser-known mayoral candidates have joined in the alarm about Chicago public safety despite the city’s historically low violent crime numbers.</p><p>Johnson links the improved numbers to his selection of Larry Snelling as police superintendent, Chicago’s focus on CTA safety and its investments in community violence intervention and youth summer jobs.</p><p>But some of his challengers have suggested Johnson doesn’t deserve much credit because the downward murder trend began in 2022, the year before his mayoral tenure began, and because murder numbers have been falling in cities across the country.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-8a0000" name="html-embed-module-8a0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30107083"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30107083/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>“In the current environment, Brandon is going to be dismissed,” political strategist Delmarie Cobb said. “But if crime is down everywhere, then who’s responsible for it? Is Trump correct? Is the president responsible, or are the local elected officials?”</p><p>Former Chicago Ald. Dick Simpson, a retired University of Illinois Chicago political scientist, said Chicagoans “still don’t feel like they’re completely safe.”</p><p>“They will still see spikes from day to day or week to week, where additional crimes have been committed,” Simpson said. “There may be weekends where more people are killed, and so it will still be an issue about whether or not enough is being done to prevent crime.</p><p>“I think [Johnson will] have some difficulty in answering it. He has the facts on his side … but for the average voter, they’re not interested in the statistics.”</p><p>Northwestern University political scientist Jaime Dominguez said Johnson is in a “good position to really take credit for what his administration has been doing in terms of, overall, bringing those crime numbers down.”</p><p>Still, Dominguez acknowledged, “perception is a reality.”</p><p>“The perception of these roving teens getting together and creating chaos and mayhem in the Loop and around Grant Park, that perception becomes a reality,” he said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/01/chicago-crime-murder-homicide-shooting-president-trump-mayor-johnson" target="_blank" >Chicago records fewest killings since 1965, despite Trump’s campaign against city</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/public-safety/2026/01/14/mayor-brandon-johnson-touts-lower-crime-community-orgs-say-lack-of-funding-jeopardizes-the-trend" target="_blank" >As mayor touts lower crime, community groups say lack of funding jeopardizes the trend</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/crime/2026/06/22/local-leaders-advocates-department-of-gun-violence-reduction" target="_blank" >Chicago government leaders, advocates call for creation of a city Department of Gun Violence Reduction</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Ye is unrecognizable from the ‘Old Kanye’
entries.summary: <p>When I was a homesick, young college student, miles and miles away from Chicago, it was the music video of an up-and-coming young rapper named Kanye West that made me feel closer to home.</p><p>I remember staring longingly, in Florida, at a TV screen airing “Through the Wire.” The video took viewers to all of my favorite high school hangs: the Halsted Mall; my personal favorite Harold’s Chicken location at the time on 103rd; places that now made my South Side world feel magnified on a world stage.</p><p>And then there was the song itself. Nothing is more Chicago than a story about pushing through a car accident to literally rap through a mouth wired shut. I was hooked.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/uvb-1wjAtk4?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Kanye West - Through The Wire"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>But more than that, I was enamored with the creativity, lightness and fun of the entire “College Dropout” album. I was loving college life, and here I was, diving into an album about also dropping out of it.</p><p>The irony of it all: It was clear that Kanye, the son of a beloved Chicago college professor, was more than capable of going to college if he so wanted. In it, there was a defiance — a creative distinctiveness I learned was also one of the reasons I probably loved my favorite Jay-Z album, “The Blueprint.”</p><p>With albums like “808s & Heartbreak” to “My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy,” I’d spend hours dissecting every lyric, every sample, every artistic choice. A mad genius who pushed the envelope with his work is always more fun to study than someone who plays it safe.</p><p>And at the time, Kanye’s bravado and confidence was a comfort in a world that had pushed respectability on Black millennials like me. After Hurricane Katrina landed, I watched thousands of people who looked like me left helpless: in flooded waters, stuck on rooftops, hungry and in need of food. Next to that imagery came photographs of our nation’s commander-in-chief, looking down at a flooded New Orleans from the comfort of Air Force One.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-portrait-right> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ec0000" name="image-ec0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium-3x4"> <source type="image/webp" width="375" height="500" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/747cd86/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1251x1668+625+0/resize/375x500!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2F7f%2F93f6828a4e4bae740ab4a423bc4c%2Fye-essay-1-260903-04.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSI1MDBweCIgd2lkdGg9IjM3NXB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="375" height="500" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ee93e73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1251x1668+625+0/resize/375x500!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2F7f%2F93f6828a4e4bae740ab4a423bc4c%2Fye-essay-1-260903-04.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSI1MDBweCIgd2lkdGg9IjM3NXB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Arionne Nettles, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. " width="375" height="500" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ee93e73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1251x1668+625+0/resize/375x500!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2F7f%2F93f6828a4e4bae740ab4a423bc4c%2Fye-essay-1-260903-04.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSI1MDBweCIgd2lkdGg9IjM3NXB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Arionne Nettles. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>So, when Kanye said on live TV, “George Bush doesn’t care about Black people,” he said what many Black folks were thinking: the federal government had stranded a city of its own filled with Black people.</p><p>But years later, his outspokenness changed from being the voice of others to a cloudy, indistinguishable mess — and with it came my own disappointment. He called slavery “a choice,” handed out White Lives Matter shirts at his Yeezy label’s fashion week shows in Paris, went on antisemitic tirades and even sold a shirt with a swastika.</p><p>I don’t believe in trying too hard to make sense of words and actions that are simply harmful, nor do I tell people how to think or feel about celebrities. But somewhere between the fame and the connections, or — as many fans argue —<a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/02/02/nx-s1-5692924/looking-at-yes-apology-through-a-bipolar-disorder-lens" target="_blank" ><u> the mental illness</u></a> and the death of his mother, Kanye has become unrecognizable from the creative we fell in love with.</p><p>But here’s the complication many fans are now in: Whoever he is today, and regardless of who he may continue to become, music — and Chicago music, specifically — has been forever changed by his presence.</p><p>He mentored <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2023/04/28/chance-the-rapper-acid-rap-mixtape-chicago-impact" target="_blank" ><u>Chance the Rapper.</u></a> He spotlighted people like GLC and Consequence. He collaborated (both in music and in community work) with Rhymefest. He put prodigious fashion designer Virgil Abloh on center stage in more ways than one. So many people and institutions were touched by Kanye, his talent, or his fame throughout the decades.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> his presence, including putting prodigious fashion designer Virgil Abloh (right) on center stage.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>I don’t listen to Kanye’s new music. While I don’t think any artist can be perfect, I’m a person who is either inspired by or turned off by what they do outside of the recording booth. And his creative choices today are weighty, dark and lack the delight that made me fall in love with his music in the first place.</p><p>But when I’m somewhere, and “Through the Wire” comes on, a smile so big it takes over my entire face appears, and it is uncontrollable. And the warm memories of the “Old Kanye” many of us remember are still there. As he returns to Chicago and his old stomping ground, during what seems to be a literal apology tour, we’ll see if — for many fans — those feelings only exist in a collective consciousness.</p><p><i>Arionne Nettles is a news editor for WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times. She is the author of “We Are the Culture: Black Chicago’s Influence on Everything” and “Journalism for Dummies.” Follow her on </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/arionnenettles/" target="_blank" ><i>Instagram</i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: How did a native Chicago plant disappear forever?
entries.summary: <p>Sandwiched between a railyard and a Ford assembly plant lie 150 acres of native ecosystem: Indian Ridge Marsh Park. Here in the South Deering neighborhood, birdsong harmonizes with the lowing of a train as we walk into the soggy prairie. The grass is up to our shoulders. The ground is thick with native plants. The mud pulls at our shoes. We’re searching for something smaller than a penny: Thismia americana.</p><p>“The vegetation looks nice and lush,” says Trevor Edmonson, restoration ecologist with The Nature Conservancy in Indiana. “We’re here at the right time. The weather seems to be right. Why not?”</p><p>Thismia americana is a tiny, blue-white flower first discovered in Chicago in 1912. By 1916, the plant had vanished, never to be seen in the wild again. Still, scientists like Edmonson search for it, despite the odds.</p><p>Why, after more than a century, do scientists continue to look? The disappearance of Thismia americana tells scientists how humans have changed the environment, but the ongoing search for the plant finds hope in restoration efforts.</p><h3><b>Origins of a mystery</b></h3><p>The last remaining Thismia americana specimens<i> </i>are housed in the Field Museum’s Botanical Collections. It’s locked up along with other federally regulated flowering plants — coca, cannabis, opium poppy.</p><p>“We keep our Thismia in here just because people get very excited about it, and we’re excited that people are excited about plants,” says Kimberly Hansen, collections manager for flowering plants.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In 2011, a search party, organized by the Field Museum, hunted the Thismia americana. Samples of the plant are kept in the museum’s Botanical Collections.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times Media</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In alcohol, Thismia americana looks like a translucent orb with thin, alien appendages poised above a bulbous flower. Its characteristics are strange too: Unlike most plants, those in the Thismia genus don’t photosynthesize; they get their energy from fungi instead of sunlight, which leads to them flowering only sporadically. These samples were donated by Thismia americana’s discoverer herself, Norma Pfeiffer.</p><p>In 1912, then a botany student at the University of Chicago, she was collecting moss in a swampy prairie at what is now 119th Street and Torrence Avenue when she happened upon this small, strange plant.</p><p>At the time of Pfeiffer’s discovery, there were only 18 known species in the Thismia genus, the most similar being Thismia rodwayi, a plant native to Australia and New Zealand. Thismia americana was the first of its genus found in the Northern Hemisphere.</p><p>Pfeiffer studied Thismia americana from 1912 to 1914. For her work, she received her PhD from the University of Chicago at 24 — the youngest PhD recipient in the school’s history at the time.</p><p>However, in 1914, Pfeiffer reported a barn was built atop the site where Thismia americana was found. According to a journal entry, Pfeiffer last saw the plant in 1916.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Norma Pfeiffer pollinating lilies, date unknown. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of The Boyce Thompson Institute</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Because Thismia americana’s story is so strange, some have speculated it<i> </i>is an elaborate botanical conspiracy.</p><p>“I’ve heard the theory that it was brought in by ballast waters from a ship that was traveling from East Asia that passed through Lake Michigan and came into Lake Calumet,” says Katie Kucera, lead ecologist at the Chicago-based Wetlands Initiative. “I don’t know if I believe the ballast water theory.”</p><p>Like Kucera, most scientists believe it’s unlikely Thismia americana came and went by nefarious means. Really, it was lost because of industry around the Calumet region.</p><p>“We’re very unlikely to ever find Thismia [americana] there again, because the history of that site is that it was a wetland complex, and then humans filled it in with a bunch of construction debris, soil, concrete, slag from the steel industry,” says Harry Kuttner, Calumet program manager at the Wetlands Initiative.</p><p>Nevertheless, scientists hope that Thismia americana could be found again. Over the past decades, organizations around Chicago have taken steps to restore the city’s green spaces, including Indian Ridge Marsh Park, where Thismia americana was discovered.</p><h3><b>Thismia in a haystack</b></h3><p>In 1948, armed with a map gifted by Pfeiffer herself. Chicago botanist Floyd Swink went hunting for the plant. Not only did he fail to find it, but he lost Pfeiffer’s map. That was the first in a long-running but infrequent tradition of Thismia-hunting in the region.</p><p>By the 1990s, these Thismia hunts came with a measure of fanfare. For instance, one hunt included a slow, gentle drumming that came from the woods. “We all filed back along the little woodland trail,” says Gerry Wilhelm, botanist with the Conservation Research Institute. “As we approached the little glade where we were instructed to go, Norma Pfeiffer emerged.”</p><p>There, she handed out paper Thismia specimens to the hunters. This wasn’t actually Norma Pfeiffer, who passed away in 1989, but an actor dressed as the botanist.</p><p>During another hunt, scientists scattered hundreds of small white beads into the prairie to train people’s eyes as they searched for Thismia americana. After the hunters were told where to look, they still could not find all of them. Today, a Thismia hunter is perhaps as likely to find a Thismia bead as the long-lost flower.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure At Indian Ridge Marsh Park, several aptly named plants command our attention: gray-headed coneflower, northern blue flag iris, cardinal flower, swamp rose mallow. Part of searching for Thismia americana isn’t just about looking for a plant that no one alive has seen, but for the plants that indicate it could be nearby, like common boneset or swamp milkweed. Once we find the correct indicators, we slow down.</p><p>“Little flowers off the mint also are good mimics, not to mention all the little shells and anything white that’s small,” Edmonson says.</p><p>He pauses at a small, bell-shaped flower. It looks ”so much like Thismia,” he says. Sadly, it is a flower off the obedient plant, a type of mint.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink"
